**Why this is the right shape.** We already have the rule "a $context-bound tile whose role is unwired hides itself" — that's how the hide-unwired doctrine works everywhere. So your #2 falls out almost for free: `source_select` becomes a sixth role alongside media_player / dpad / power / volume / volume_level. The stock controllers carry a Source tile bound to `$context.source_select`, and the tile exists *if and only if* some device in the activity's Setup carries that role. No new conditional logic — the same rule that hides the Volume tile when nothing's wired to volume. Assign the role to the Samsung in the watch activities and the TV controller grows a full-width "Source · Fire TV" tile; assign it to nothing and the tile simply isn't there. Yesterday's title-bar input button dies — you're right that a bar icon is a fingertip-hostile target on the Astrion, and I'd remove `info_button` outright rather than leave two ways to do one thing. It's a day old; kill it before it calcifies.

**Your #1 — cast curation.** The overlap you're seeing is structural: the Devices section is generated from the cast, but the cast members are mostly *already on the page* as role-driven tiles (the Samsung is the Volume tile, the Fire TV is Now Playing). So the Devices section re-lists what the controller already controls. A per-device "shows in Devices" toggle next to the ★, default on, puts the curation where it belongs — in Setup, which is already the single place that declares what an activity involves. Existing configs render identically until you start switching things off.

**Data shape** (for discussion, not code): I'd keep the device list as-is and store the toggle as a sidecar — something like `device_options: {entity: {tile: false}}` on the activity — rather than turning each device entry into an object. That's additive, needs no migration, and your Setup snippets keep working unchanged.

Decisions I'd like your call on:

1. **Does the visibility checkbox also gate the Source tile?** Your "if and only if a source select device exists and the checkbox is on" could read either way. My instinct: keep them orthogonal — the checkbox curates the *Devices section* only; the Source tile is governed purely by the role. Otherwise hiding the Samsung's (redundant) device tile would also kill its Source tile, which is probably the one thing you *do* want from it.

2. **Where does the Source tile sit?** I'd put it in the stock controllers' main stack (after Volume), not inside the Devices section — it's a control, not a cast listing. Custom controllers place it wherever, as now.

3. **Music controller:** retarget the m_src tile from `$context.media_player` to `$context.source_select` so it obeys the same rule — you'd assign the role to the Sonos (or the amp) in the music activity's Setup. Consistent, at the cost of one role assignment before it reappears.

4. **The toggle's face:** a checkbox next to ★ per your spec, or an eye icon (👁) which reads as "visible" without a label? Same behavior either way.

Every so often all my theme settings are reset - is that to be expected?

CLAUDE  2026-07-26T19:03:42.673Z
========================================================================

Yes — and it's a design flaw biting you, not a bug. Now that you've asked, I can tell you exactly when it happens: **every time we run the deploy ceremony.**

Here's the mechanism. The main workspace has *two* authors: the repo (my yaml, compiled to config.json) and you (Studio → Save & Deploy, which writes the server store). `harmonium.reseed` declares the repo the winner — it overwrites the whole stored main config with the repo build. Your theme tuning was done in the Studio, so it lives only in the store, never in the repo yaml. Every reseed wipes it back to the repo's theme. Same is true for *any* Studio-side change to Main — theme is just where you notice, because we reseed on nearly every engine batch and your fonts snap back. (Your other workspaces don't have this problem — they have no repo counterpart, so reseed never touches their content. And this is the parked "yaml round-trip" gap from the decisions log, finally drawing blood.)

Two-part fix I'd propose:

**Right now — make your theme repo-truth.** Re-apply your theme settings in the Studio once (fonts, sizes, icon zone, bar size — however you had them) and hit Save & Deploy. Then say the word and I'll read the deployed config off HA, lift the whole `theme` block into the repo yaml, and from then on reseed *carries* your theme instead of erasing it. Same offer stands anytime you make a Studio-side change to Main you want to be permanent — tell me "harvest it" and I'll fold it into the yaml.

**Structurally — a safety net so reseed can never destroy work again.** Make reseed snapshot the outgoing main config to a `config.main.backup.json` beside the live one before overwriting, plus a `harmonium.restore_backup` service. One-deep undo: if a reseed ever eats something, we get it back instead of mourning it. Small Python change; I'd fold it into the next batch (it'll need one HA restart).

Longer term the real cure is the yaml round-trip (Studio saves flow back into the repo), which stays on the roadmap — the harvest-on-request habit covers us until then.

Want me to prep the safety net now, or wait until you've re-applied the theme so I can harvest it in the same pass?

SURESH  2026-07-26T19:06:40.405Z
========================================================================

Why do we need to zap it in the first place? Is it because we've changed the json and need to reflect those changes?

========================================================================
CLAUDE  2026-07-26T19:07:08.762Z
========================================================================

Exactly right — reseed exists only to *reflect repo changes*. The wrinkle is who reads what: the remotes read `config.json` directly, so your bat alone updates them. But the Studio and the integration's services (`harmonium.run`, `set_activity`) read the *store*. Without a reseed after a repo push, the Studio shows you a stale config and — worse — a hold-Power runs the *old* All Off sequence. So the store has to be brought up to date.

The zap isn't necessary, though — it's just the crude way we do it. Reseed does a wholesale replace because we've never tracked *provenance*: looking at the store and the new repo build, we can't tell "Suresh changed the theme in the Studio" apart from "the repo changed the theme," so we punt and let the repo win everything.

But there's a well-known cure that doesn't need the full yaml round-trip: a **three-way merge**. Reseed keeps a snapshot of the repo build it last seeded (the *base*). Next reseed, it computes two diffs — base→new repo (what I changed) and base→store (what you changed in the Studio) — and applies both to produce the new store. Your theme edits survive because the repo *didn't touch* theme relative to base; my new Source tile lands because you didn't touch the tv controller. Only a genuine conflict (we both changed the same key) needs a rule, and there "repo wins, and log what it overrode" is the sane default — plus the one-deep backup file so nothing is ever unrecoverable.

The pleasant side effect: deploy ceremonies stop being destructive *at all*. You could tune in the Studio for a week, I could ship five engine batches, and both streams just coexist — the repo yaml drifting from your Studio-authored parts stops mattering day-to-day (harvesting into yaml becomes housekeeping, not survival).

Cost: a merge routine in the integration (pure-Python, unit-testable like `workspaces.py`), the base snapshot riding in the store, the backup file, and a `harmonium.restore_backup` escape hatch. One HA restart to land it.

Want it? If yes I'll build it now — and once it's in, you re-apply your theme once and it's the last time you ever do.

CLAUDE  2026-07-26T23:24:39.917Z
========================================================================

Deployed — Astrion's reloading, hard-refresh the Studio tab. Now the URL question, because your instinct is pointing at something real.

**What the current strategy is: identity-in-the-device.** A remote is whichever workspace its localStorage says, set once by a magic hash. That was borrowed from `#device=` — and for *device profiles* it's correct, because "I have a physical D-pad" genuinely is a property of the device. But a workspace isn't a property of the device — it's an *address in the world*. Storing it invisibly means the answer to "why is this tablet showing Bedroom?" lives somewhere you can't see. Six months from now, a kiosk misbehaving after a cache wipe or a swap-out means remembering that a hidden pin exists at all. That's the constraint: not capability (the peek link already lets you open two workspaces side by side), but *legibility*. The system's whole doctrine is "dumb renderer, no hidden state" — and the pin is hidden state.

**What paths buy: identity-in-the-address.** `/local/remote-proto/deck/` says everything on its face. A remote is whatever URL Fully is told to load — provisioning is just "set the start URL," which you're doing anyway. Bookmarkable, shareable, debuggable from the address bar, survives storage wipes, and matches the mental model: worlds get addresses.

**The trap to avoid** is the naive implementation: one engine *copy* per workspace path. That fans out deployment — N copies of index.html to cache-bust, version skew where the porch runs v0.37 and the deck runs v0.35 — and it's why I didn't do paths originally. But there's a version with none of that cost: the engine stays one file in one place, and the integration writes a **tiny stub** per workspace — `www/remote-proto/deck/index.html`, ~3 lines, which immediately hands off to the shared engine with the right workspace. Stubs are created and deleted by the same workspace CRUD that already writes `config.deck.json`; they never change when the engine updates, so there's nothing to keep in sync. Fully's start URL becomes the pretty path and the pin mechanism becomes unnecessary for kiosks entirely (it can stay as a compatibility fallback; `#device=` remains, since that one really is device state).

Small print: the path would use the workspace *id* (rename stays display-only, as now); `/local/remote-proto/` bare remains Main so the Astrion never notices; and mid-use the address bar would show the handoff form rather than the pretty path — the pretty path is the *entry point*, which is where legibility matters (start URLs, bookmarks, the Studio link).

**My verdict:** current scheme = functional but illegible; paths = same capability, self-documenting, *more* aligned with your architecture than what I built. I'd do it — it's a small batch (integration writes/removes stubs, Studio link and Workspaces-page hints show paths). Say go and it's in the next lift.

CLAUDE  2026-07-27T16:21:15.465Z
========================================================================

Congratulations on the milestone — and this is the right moment to ask, because polish work is exactly what you do *after* the architecture stops moving. Let me split the question the way it deserves, because "not intuitive" and "not attractive" are different diseases with different medicine.

**First, the honest diagnosis.** *Attractive* is a visual-design problem: tokens, type ramp, spacing rhythm, component states, color discipline. *Intuitive* is an information-architecture problem: the Studio's dense nav pane, concertinas-inside-concertinas, tiny glyph buttons (you've hit these — the ⤴/⤵ episode), JSON escape hatches, and no onboarding affordances. Tools like Figma help with the first; the second is mostly design *thinking* applied to flows, and no tool does it for you.

**On your three candidates:**

**Claude Design (Anthropic Labs)** — this is real and, from what I can see, a genuinely good fit for your situation. It launched in early 2026 as an AI-native design/prototyping tool that can read an existing codebase and generate visual directions consistent with it, and as of mid-2026 it round-trips with Claude Code — design there, hand the result back to code ([Anthropic announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs), [product page](https://claude.com/product/design), [VentureBeat on the design-system-import + code round-trip overhaul](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropic-ships-major-claude-design-overhaul-with-design-system-imports-code-round-trips-and-a-fix-for-its-token-burning-problem), [Claude Code integration](https://theplanettools.ai/blog/claude-design-claude-code-integration-2026)). Since your repo is now on GitHub, you could point it at the Studio and ask for visual directions — its sweet spot is exactly the divergent *exploration* that's slow to do through chat with me.

**Figma** — the classic, but I'd say skip it here. Its value is when a human designer is doing the crafting; for you it adds a manual translation layer between picture and Svelte with no safety net. Everything Figma would give you, Claude Design gives you closer to the code.

**Me** — I'm not the exploration layer; I'm the *implementation and protection* layer, and that's the part that answers "without breaking all this good work." I know every component, the state contracts, and the 12 suites; I restyle surface-by-surface with tests green and screenshot-verify each change (as we did with the State header). One more ace we're sitting on: the Studio already runs bits-ui + tailwind-variants + tailwind-merge — that's literally the shadcn-svelte stack — so adopting shadcn-svelte's polished component patterns is a facelift with near-zero architectural risk.

**My recommended pipeline:** (1) You gather taste — either run the Studio through Claude Design for 2–3 visual directions, or just collect screenshots of UIs you love (Linear and Raycast are the usual north stars for this genre). (2) We pick one and I distill it into a design-token system and component spec. (3) I apply it incrementally — one editor per batch, suites green, before/after screenshots to you. (4) Separately, a UX pass on the flows: progressive disclosure in the nav, honest empty states, bigger touch targets, fewer glyphs-without-labels. That last track is where "intuitive" actually gets fixed, and it's discussion-first — same as the workspaces doctrine was.

Sources: [Introducing Claude Design by Anthropic Labs](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs), [Claude Design product page](https://claude.com/product/design), [VentureBeat: Claude Design overhaul](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropic-ships-major-claude-design-overhaul-with-design-system-imports-code-round-trips-and-a-fix-for-its-token-burning-problem), [Claude Design + Claude Code integration](https://theplanettools.ai/blog/claude-design-claude-code-integration-2026), [DataCamp: What Is Claude Design?](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/claude-design), [How good is Claude Design? CLAUDE  2026-07-27T17:41:43.456Z

Keep both words — but stop letting them trespass on each other. Here's my thinking.

"Device" and "tile" live at different layers, and that difference is real, not accidental. **Device is domain vocabulary** — the nouns you own: the Samsung, the Sonos, the Fire TV. It's what activities cast, what roles wire, what Harmony taught twenty years of users to say. **Tile is presentation vocabulary** — the atomic unit of a page grid. *Everything* on a page is a tile: activity tiles, preset tiles, nav cards, transport bars, volume rows… and yes, device tiles. A blanket rename to "tiles" would flatten that: "Setup — tiles & roles" is obviously wrong, because an activity doesn't involve *tiles*, it involves *devices*. And going the other way — calling every tile a "device" — is worse. So the ambiguity you're sensing isn't that we have two words; it's that we're not disciplined about which word appears where.

The rule I'd adopt: **devices are what you own; tiles are how things show up on a page.** Whenever the UI means the physical thing (cast, roles, Setup, the entity picker), say device. Whenever it means the rectangle on the grid, say tile — and "device tile" is the honest compound for the rectangle that shows a device. This keeps the Harmony paradigm fully intact where it matters (Activities vs Devices as the user's mental model) while giving the page editor a clean word for its unit of layout.

Where today's UI actually violates the rule — three spots, all small:

1. **The tile Type dropdown** is the worst offender: it offers `device` *and* `devices` — singular is one tile, plural is the cast *generator* that auto-lists an activity's devices. Nobody could guess that. The generator should be relabeled something like **"Cast (auto)"** — it's not "devices," it's "the activity's devices, kept in sync."
2. **That same dropdown mixes layers**: content types (device, nav, activity, preset, apps, sources) alongside raw renderers (light, media, volume, dpad…). The raw ones are really *widgets* — an advanced sub-group, maybe literally labeled "Raw widgets," or tucked behind a disclosure.
3. **"＋ Add device" next to "＋ Add nav card"** names one button by content and the other by form. Defensible as intent-speak (users think "put my TV on this page"), so I'd leave the wording — but it's worth knowing it's the same act: both add tiles.

One timing note: the design brief froze terminology so Claude Design doesn't invent its own — which means *now* is exactly the moment to settle this, before mockups bake words in. My proposal: keep Devices (Harmony-aligned), keep Tiles (layout unit), rename the `devices` generator's label to "Cast (auto)," and group the Type list into Content / Raw widgets. That's a 20-minute Studio-labels batch with zero engine or config changes — say go and it's in before the design round lands.

CLAUDE  2026-07-27T17:45:47.273Z
========================================================================

You've found the vestige, and you're right that it's a flaw — but the good news is it's a flaw in *presentation*, not structure. Let me separate what the system actually is from what the labels claim.

**Structurally, sections are already type-agnostic.** A page is a list of sections; a section is a title plus a bag of tiles; *any* tile type can live in *any* section. Your porch proves it: the so-called "Devices" section holds two device tiles and a nav card, and the engine doesn't care. The only tiles with real magic are the **generators** — the activities generator and the cast generator — and their magic travels *with the tile*, not with the section it sits in. So there is no "Devices section" type in the engine. There are sections, and one of yours happens to be titled "Devices."

**The lie lives in two places.** First, the `role:` field (`activities` / `presets` / `devices`) — which sounds like a type system but is actually just soft plumbing: it tells the Studio where the "＋ Add device" button should drop tiles, and it seeds default hero labels in the starter. Second, and worse, the Studio *presents* that plumbing as taxonomy — the canonical "Devices" fold in the editor implies the section is *for* devices, when really it's "the general tile area that the starter happened to name Devices." That's the confusion you're feeling: Activities and Presets sections mostly do contain what they say, so the third label reads as a category too — and it isn't.

**What I'd do — demote, don't rename:**

1. **Sections become just "sections with titles"** in the Studio's presentation: every fold header shows the section's *authored title* (fully editable), never a role-derived category. "Devices" on your porch becomes merely the name you gave that section — rename it "Shortcuts" or "Everything else" tomorrow and nothing breaks, because nothing ever depended on it.
2. **`role:` gets demoted to invisible plumbing** — it keeps doing its one useful job (default target for the add buttons, starter labels) but never surfaces as a concept. Long-term it could disappear entirely in favor of "add buttons target the section whose fold you're in," which is more honest anyway.
3. **The typed things remain the tiles**: device tile, nav card, preset, activity tile, generators. Which lands exactly on the rule from last message — *devices are what you own, tiles are how things show up, and sections are just named shelves.*

One nuance to keep: on **controllers**, the Devices section really is special-ish — it's where the cast generator conventionally lives, and "Devices" is the honest title for a cast listing. But note that's the *generator tile* earning the title, not a section type. Same rule, no exception needed.

This folds neatly into the terminology batch already on the table (Cast (auto) rename, Content/Raw-widgets grouping in the Type list) — and it's another thing worth settling before Claude Design mockups bake labels in. Want me to run that batch — section-titles-as-headers, role demoted, Type-list cleanup — as one "taxonomy honesty" pass?

You're right, and this is a better argument than mine. I was solving for internal consistency; you're solving for *paradigm fidelity* — and Harmonium exists precisely because Harmony's paradigm was good. Let me reverse the frame properly.

**The principle you're stating:** generality belongs to the engine, opinion belongs to the user experience. We built a maximally general substrate — any tile, any section, any page — and that's *why* the system is powerful. But the substrate leaking into the user's face as "sections of tiles" is a category error. A Harmony user never thought "tiles." They thought: *I have Devices. I create Activities from them. I get one-touch Presets.* That liturgy is the product. My "demote everything to named shelves" suggestion was the engineer's move — making the UI as general as the engine, just because we can. Wrong direction.

**So flip it: paradigm-first, generality behind glass.**

A **room hub** isn't "a page with sections" — it *is* the liturgy: **Activities → Presets → Devices**, presented as blessed, typed zones with paradigm verbs on them: ＋ Add activity, ＋ Add preset, ＋ Add device. Not "add a tile of type…" — nobody adds tiles; they add *things from their life*. The generic machinery (custom sections, raw widget types, the Type dropdown, JSON) stays fully available but retreats to an "advanced" layer — the escape hatch you reach for deliberately, not the default face.

And notice your nav-card "flaw" resolves *inside* the paradigm rather than by generalizing it away: the HVAC & Lights card in your Devices zone isn't a misfiled tile — it's a **doorway to more devices**. The Devices zone holds your devices *and doorways to them*. That's semantically honest and needs no new category. (Controllers get the same treatment: their liturgy is the control stack — Now Playing, Transport, Volume, Source, then the cast under "Devices" — which is exactly what they already are.)

**Terminology fallout:** "Device" stays the user-facing word everywhere, full Harmony alignment. "Tile" retreats to implementation vocabulary — the advanced layer and the docs — instead of being promoted. My earlier suggestions survive only in demoted form: "Cast (auto)" and the Content/Raw-widget grouping live *inside* the escape hatch, where the people who open it can handle them.

One concrete, timely action: this stance belongs in the design brief before Claude Design starts sketching — it's the single most important instruction we could give it, and it wasn't there. I'd add a short section: *"Design principle: paradigm-first. The user's world is Devices, Activities, Presets, Rooms. Room pages present the fixed liturgy Activities → Presets → Devices as blessed zones with paradigm verbs; the generalized machinery (sections, tile types, JSON) is an advanced layer, deliberately behind glass. Never surface the word 'tile' on a primary path."* Want me to amend the brief now, before you feed it in? The Studio-side restructuring itself (zones with paradigm add-verbs, advanced layer) I'd hold until the design round lands — it's exactly the kind of IA change the mockups should incorporate rather than chase.

Studied the whole package — README spec, component specs, implementation plan, tokens.css, and the mocks. Verdict first: **this is an unusually implementable handoff, and the designer took §5 seriously.** The paradigm survived contact — four blessed sections with paradigm verbs, doorways as "devices that lead to more devices," the vocabulary table literally bans "tile/zone/slice" from the primary path, and Advanced-behind-glass is a designed object (that glass tab treatment), not an afterthought. Later turns even use your *real* entities and *real* roles (`media_player.sts_samsung_q90_porch`, `source_select`), so someone actually read the config. The self-correcting README (§7.3 "where the mocks and I disagree, I win") and the open-questions list are good hygiene. Graphite Rails itself is right: quiet, hairline, amber-only — Linear-adjacent without being a clone.

**The four best structural ideas**, in my order of value: (1) the **one item-card grammar** — identity strip on every tab, per-type tab sets, Advanced always last — dissolves your #1 pain point (ActivityCard overload) with *one* component we refactor onto, exactly matching our primitives list; (2) **blessed sections with switches and counts** — the liturgy made physical, and "off ≠ empty" is genuinely smart; (3) **source chips for inheritance** (`FROM THEME` / `SET HERE` + Reset) — this is your parked "per-page overrides" ambition given a UI language; (4) the **Workspace map** landing screen — read-only, built from existing config, and it makes multi-workspace households legible.

**Where the designer didn't know the detail — the gaps we must resolve before building:**

1. **The POWER column is invented.** Devices & roles shows FACE·SHOW·POWER switches; FACE maps to our ★ primary and SHOW to the 👁 visibility toggle, but per-device "power" participation doesn't exist in our model — power scope is derived or authored in sequences. Options: drop the column for v1 (my recommendation), or adopt it as a real feature later ("include in derived power-off"), which is a config change.
2. **The sizing cascade outruns the engine.** Theme → Workspace → Page → Section → Item is beautiful, but the engine today has global theme height/gap, page/section *columns*, and item span — no per-section tile height, no per-page gap. V1 should show source chips only for knobs that actually exist; the full cascade is a *joint engine+Studio* batch later, not a Studio restyle.
3. **Section on/off switches need a config key** (`enabled: false` per section) plus engine skip — tiny and merge-safe, but it contradicts their own "no config-model change" guardrail, so it's our call: I'd add it, it's cheap and the "off ≠ empty" behavior is worth it.
4. **Hero-as-a-section is a mapping fiction** — our banner is page-level config. Fine: the Hero "section" becomes a presentation grouping over banner settings; no model change.
5. **Sundry mock drift** the README mostly already corrects: turn-2a's tab set and role names are superseded; Drawer|Push on doorways is actually a property of the *target page*, not the tile; the preset "belongs to activity" sentence conflates warm-start gating with page placement — copy needs care there.
6. **Their §8 questions need answers from you** — my proposed answers: span stays per-item (no forced uniform widths); 3-across is the practical kiosk ceiling but don't hard-limit; page-level rules = grid + keys + banner, nothing more for now; yes, app class stays on the activity; span controls hide in 1-column sections (their own "hidden, not disabled" rule).

**On sequencing** — their phase order is right, with two amendments. Phase 1 (tokens) must not be a big-bang rename: 28 Svelte files use the old utility names (`bg-tile`, `text-dim`…), so I'd land the new tokens *with the old names aliased*, keep all 12 suites green, then migrate names file-by-file as each phase touches them. And phase 5 (the item-card grammar) is the riskiest — it refactors ActivityCard/TileRow/CardRow onto one component, which means test updates in the same commits; I'd want phases 1–4 deployed and settled on your Astrion first, since each phase is independently shippable via the light ceremony (studio.html only).

Decisions I need from you: **drop or adopt the POWER column** for v1 · **add the section `enabled` key** or defer · **sizing subset v1** (chips only where real) with the full cascade as a later engine batch · **Workspace map as the default landing screen** yes/no · and blessing of the phase order with my two amendments. Then we start with tokens + copy pass, which are low-risk and transform the feel on day one.

CLAUDE  2026-07-28T03:49:30.621Z
========================================================================

Here's the honest map — and the catch: only a few sizes are variable-controlled today; most are Tailwind *arbitrary values* baked into class names (`text-[13px]`), so they're per-rule in devtools, not one knob. Where things live:

**Real variables (edit on `:root` / `html` in the Styles pane):**

- `body { font: 13px/1.45 var(--font-sans) }` in the token stylesheet — the base size. Anything styled `font-[inherit]` (most buttons, inputs) rides on this, so bumping it to 14px lifts a lot of the app at once.
- `--font-sans` / `--font-mono` — the two families.
- Tailwind's named sizes are variables in v4: `--text-xs` (0.75rem/12px) and `--text-sm` (0.875rem/14px) drive every `text-xs` / `text-sm` utility. A lot of the editors' chrome (tabs, hints, buttons, status) is `text-xs`, so overriding `--text-xs: 0.8125rem` on `:root` is the single most effective experiment you can run.

**Hard-coded sizes (find the rule via the element's class, e.g. `.text-\[14px\]`, and edit it live):**

- Nav: rows 14px · child rows 13.5 · right annotations 11.5 · group headers 10.5 (uppercase, tracked) · search 13 · tokens 10.5 · STOCK/EDITED badges 9.
- Map: title 20 · summary line 13 · PAGES caption 11 · card names 16 · mono ids 11.5 · card tabs 12.5 · row names 13 · row details 12 (mono 11) · badges 9.5 · controller names 13.5 · sharing sentences 12.
- Item cards: field labels 11 uppercase (Field.svelte) · field values 13 (Input/Select, 38px tall) · card tabs 12 (`text-xs`) · mono machine values 12–12.5 · helper hints 11.

One devtools tip: since each arbitrary value is one shared CSS rule, editing `.text-\[13px\] { font-size: 14px }` in the inline stylesheet changes *every* 13px element at once — a decent way to preview a global step-up without clicking elements one by one.

And an offer: this hard-coding is a leftover; the handoff's type ramp really belongs in tokens. When your experiments settle, give me the numbers — or just say the word and I'll tokenize the whole ramp into `--fs-nav-row`, `--fs-card-title`, `--fs-annotation`, etc. in app.css so future tuning is a five-second devtools tweak (and themable per workspace later).

CLAUDE  2026-07-28T03:50:42.880Z
========================================================================

That list *was* the config UI — everything in it (nav rows, map cards, field labels) is the Studio's own chrome. Easy to conflate though, because there are two separate styling systems:

**The remote** (the phone screen): styled by `config.theme` → engine CSS vars like `--tile-h`, `--bar-fs`, `--grid-gap`. That's what the Theme editor and the Page settings Layout tab write. Not what you want here.

**The Studio** (the config UI you're in): styled by a stylesheet compiled *into* `studio.html` — nothing from `config.theme` touches it. So open devtools on the **Studio browser tab** itself, and the knobs are:

- `body` rule → `font: 13px/1.45 var(--font-sans)` — the base; everything marked `font-[inherit]` follows it. Best single experiment: change 13px → 14px on the `body` rule.
- On `:root`: `--text-xs` (12px) and `--text-sm` (14px) — these drive every `text-xs`/`text-sm` utility, which is most of the small chrome (tabs, buttons, hints, status).
- Everything else is a literal like `.text-\[14px\]` — one shared rule per size, so editing that rule in the Styles pane changes every element using it: nav rows 14, child rows 13.5, annotations 11.5, group headers 10.5, map card names 16, map title 20, row names 13, details 12, field labels 11, field values 13.

Quickest workflow: inspect any element, click its `text-[…]` rule's value, arrow-key it up and down and watch the whole class of elements move together.

When you land on numbers you like, tell me the deltas ("rows 15, annotations 12, labels 11.5" is plenty) and I'll bake them into the Studio's tokens properly.

Read both files — and first, hats off to whoever ground through that verification work: the `market://` indirection discovery, the 117-vs-84 search distinction, and the do-not-send list are exactly the kind of hard-won truth that should shape the design rather than get buried in a doc. Here's my thinking on your three questions, plus the bigger shape I think they add up to.

**The headline: these three problems are one problem.** Fire TV, Google TV, and Tizen each bring (1) their own soft keys, (2) their own transport zoo, and (3) their own idea of what a "device page" should hold. Harmonium already has a nearly-right concept for this — `app_class`, which today only answers "which apps, launched how." What the projector doc proves is that app_class wants to grow into a full **platform dialect**: apps *and* keys *and* transport rules *and* safety rails *and* quirks, per platform, with per-device overrides. Your `projector_actions.json` is accidentally a first-class dialect file already — schema'd, machine-readable, verified-flagged. I'd adopt its shape as the format rather than invent one.

**(a) Streamer keys.** They belong in the dialect as a *key catalog*: each named key carries its keycode, which transports actually deliver it (the doc's core lesson — API acceptance ≠ device behavior), and any notes ("84 = voice search, mic goes live; 117 = keyboard search"). Then the controller renders a **Keys tile/section generated from the catalog** — same pattern as the apps drawer: the dialect is the source of truth, the UI never hand-places SETTINGS or INFO per device. Only verified keys render; the `verified_noop` list keeps dead buttons out; and the **do-not-send list becomes a Studio guardrail** — those keys shouldn't even be offerable in key bindings for that dialect (nobody should be able to wire Vol-hold to `PAIRING` by accident). The search-with-typed-text recipe (117 → 6s wait → `input text the%scrown`) is a *composite* — that's a sequence template the dialect ships, not a key.

**(b) The third (really fourth) entity.** The cast already accepts multiple entities per physical device — your Fire TV rows do this today. What's missing is a role for the command channel. I'd add **one new role: `system`** (or `command`) — "the entity that takes deep commands." Wiring for the projector: `media_player` → the remote-transport media_player (instant state — the doc's "read state from remote"), `dpad` → the remote-transport remote entity, `system` → the ADB entity. Then routing is capability-driven and declared in the dialect, not hardcoded: launches and system keys go via `$context.system` when wired (falling back to today's behavior when not), state and navigation stay on the fast transport. No per-verb switches sprinkled through the UI — the dialect says "launch: adb," the role says which entity that means.

**(c) The device page.** Here's the honest observation: for a streamer, the "device page" you want *is a controller* — multi-entity, role-wired, dialect-aware. The `$device` domain stocks (Climate, Light, Fan) are right for one-entity devices and should stay. What's missing is the case of a streamer standing alone, outside any activity. And that points at the real structural gap: **"device" should become a first-class noun** — a named bundle ("Pergola TV" = these 3-4 entities with these roles + dialect `googletv`), instead of the entity being the atom. Then: the cast adds "Pergola TV" as *one row* (roles auto-wired from the bundle), the device tile's hold opens a dialect-aware page built from the bundle, and the map stops showing raw entity ids. This is a config-model addition, so it deserves its own design round — but it's where (b) and (c) both want to land, and it matches the Harmony paradigm you invoked weeks ago: users think in devices, not entities.

**Two operational notes worth deciding on separately:** the stale-`app_id`-after-standby heal (reload the config entry on wake) is a *quirk* the dialect should declare and the integration should automate — users will never diagnose that themselves; and the shared ADB key across Fire TV and the projector is a landmine worth a note in the Studio if we ever surface re-pairing.

**Decisions I'd like your ruling on:** (1) grow `app_class` into `dialect` (apps + keys + transports + quirks), using your JSON's schema? (2) one new role `system` for the command channel — or would you rather per-verb transport picks in the activity card (I think that's clutter)? (3) is first-class Devices (entity bundles) a round you want to green-light now, or do we ship dialect + `system` role first and let bundles come after? My vote: dialect + role first — it's additive, no config migration — bundles second, as their own carefully-designed round.

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T17:22:06.107Z
========================================================================

Your instinct is right, and your two examples are actually the easy case and the hard case of the same design. Let me walk both, then the UI.

**Example 1 — Porch TV as a composite device.** Today "Porch TV" on a page is a tile pointing at one entity, and everything richer about it lives, misplaced, inside whichever *activity* casts it. Your observation — "the activity page is exactly what the device page should be" — is the key, but with one refinement: they're the same *anatomy* at two different *scopes*. A **device page** answers "what can this thing do" — Now Playing, transport, volume, its inputs, its keys, its apps. An **activity page** answers "what am I doing right now" — same sections, but the cast is plural and the roles route across it (volume to the soundbar, not the TV). So we don't merge them; we make them siblings that share one grammar. The device becomes a first-class bundle: *Porch TV = these entities, these roles among themselves, dialect tizen*. And here's where your "we already have the UI" lands perfectly: the **Devices & roles table you already use in an activity IS the device-definition editor** — same rows, same role chips, same primary switch — just scoped to one device's own members instead of an activity's cast.

**Example 2 — the projector, remote + ADB.** This is the same composite, plus rules. The bundle is *Pergola TV = four entities* (remote-transport media_player + remote, ADB media_player + remote). The **roles** say who's who: `media_player` → the remote-transport one (instant state), `dpad` → the remote entity, `system` → the ADB one. The **dialect** (googletv) holds the rules your doc proved: *launch via system, system keys via system, state and navigation via the fast transport, and never send these six keycodes.* So "composite with rules" decomposes cleanly: the bundle owns the members, the roles bind them to slots, the dialect owns the routing logic — and the dialect is shared by every Google TV device you'll ever add, while the bundle is per-device. Nothing is hardcoded to your projector.

**What happens in the UI**, walking the surfaces you know:

In the **nav**, Devices join Building blocks — "what you own," beside Actions and Apps. Opening one shows the familiar table: entity rows, role chips (`media_player ×`, `dpad ×`, `system ×`), primary switch, plus a Dialect select (Fire TV · Google TV · Samsung TV · plain) up in the identity strip. Defining Pergola TV takes a minute and you've done this motion a hundred times.

In an **activity's Devices & roles tab**, the "add a device…" box offers your *defined devices first*, raw entities after. Adding "Pergola TV" adds **one row**, not four — its roles come pre-wired from the bundle (overridable: Watch Projector might route `volume` to the deck soundbar instead). Your Watch Fire TV cast today would collapse from four cryptic entity rows to two honest ones: *Fire TV* and *Porch TV* and the soundbar.

On a **page**, the device tile points at "Pergola TV." Its state line reads from the bundle's media_player role. **Hold** opens the device page — and that page is *generated from the dialect*: the media sections you have today, plus a **Keys section** (Settings, Search, All Apps, Live TV — only the verified ones; the mic-triggering voice search deliberately absent; the typed-search composite as a proper "Search…" affordance), plus the **Apps drawer** with each app launching over the transport your doc verified — BritBox simply hides if no `system` role is wired, exactly the hide-unwired doctrine we already use for Sources.

In the **Studio guardrails**: the do-not-send list means key-binding dropdowns for a googletv-dialect device never even offer `PAIRING` or the HDMI-killers; and the stale-`app_id` quirk gets declared in the dialect so the integration can auto-heal it on wake without you remembering it exists.

One collision to rule on before any of this: the config key `devices` is already taken — it holds the *remote hardware profiles* (astrion, keymaps). I'd rename that to `remotes` (which is what the nav already calls it) and give the new noun the `devices` key it deserves — a one-time migration merge3 can carry. And sequencing stays as I proposed: dialect + `system` role ship first (additive, nothing breaks), then the device bundles, then the generated device pages — each round testable on your projector, which is now the best-documented device in the house.

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T18:10:43.408Z
========================================================================

Because of which entity the service will accept — I just checked your HA's service registry directly rather than trusting memory. `androidtv.adb_command` declares its target as `{integration: androidtv, domain: [media_player]}` — the ADB integration registers that service (plus `learn_sendevent`, `download`, `upload`) on its **media_player** entity only. Point it at `remote.deck_hisense_projector_adb_192_168_1_64` and HA rejects the call before anything reaches the projector.

The two ADB entities aren't interchangeable channels; they're two different surfaces of the same integration:

- `media_player.deck_..._adb_...` — carries the polled state (volume, HDMI input, running app) **and** is the handle for `androidtv.adb_command`, which is what every entry in our dialect fires (`adb shell input keyevent 176`, `am start -n ...`). This is also what your own verified `projector_actions.json` used throughout.
- `remote.deck_..._adb_...` — a remote-platform entity that answers `remote.send_command` with key *names*. Different service, different grammar, and nothing in the googletv dialect calls it.

So the `system` role means "the entity `androidtv.adb_command` targets," and on this integration that's the media_player one. Slightly counterintuitive — a "command channel" role wired to a media_player entity — but the role names the job, and the service dictates the entity type.

One design note: Studio's SLOT_DOMAINS for `system` currently offers both `media_player` and `remote`, since a future dialect might route system keys through a remote entity (Fire TV's androidtv setup could go either way). For Google TV, the media_player ADB entity is the correct pick, and wiring the remote one would leave the key tiles rendered but every press failing. When the dialect goes machine-read in the bundles round, that's exactly the kind of thing it should validate at wiring time — flag the wrong-domain pick before you're standing in front of a projector wondering why Settings does nothing.

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T18:14:12.737Z
========================================================================

No — and I just pulled the entity registry from your HA to be sure. Same physical projector, but Home Assistant genuinely sees **two separate devices**, from two separate integrations:

| | `media_player.deck_hisense_projector` (+ `remote.…`) | `media_player.deck_hisense_projector_adb_192_168_1_64` |
|---|---|---|
| Integration | `androidtv_remote` (Android TV Remote protocol) | `androidtv` (ADB) |
| Config entry | `01KYMSWC…` | `01KYQBCR…` |
| HA device | `5a9b002b…` | `4e94164e…` |
| Unique ID | MAC `38:1b:9e:a3:fb:a9` | `a0:00:4c:c0:7d:ac` |

They don't even share a MAC in the registry (the two integrations identify the device differently), so HA has no idea these are the same projector. Nothing links them — no shared device entry, no shared binding. The only place that knowledge exists is *your activity's cast*, which is exactly the point of the roles: **the activity is the thing that says "these four entities are one device."**

That's why the wiring looks the way it does:

- **media_player** → `media_player.deck_hisense_projector` — the `androidtv_remote` one, because its state is instant push.
- **dpad** → `remote.deck_hisense_projector` — same integration, navigation keys.
- **system** → `media_player.deck_hisense_projector_adb_192_168_1_64` — the *other* integration's media_player, because that's the only entity `androidtv.adb_command` will accept.

So two media_player entities for one projector, each doing the one job the other can't: the remote one reads state, the ADB one takes commands. Your reference doc's rule of thumb ("launch and command over ADB; read state from the remote entity") maps one-to-one onto the roles.

And this is precisely the seam the phase-2 device bundle closes: a **Pergola Projector** device that bundles all four entities with their roles once, so an activity just casts *the device* instead of you re-explaining to every activity which of the two media_players is which.

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T18:17:17.967Z
========================================================================

Right — and let's untangle "slow" first, because it matters to the design. The ADB integration is slow at exactly one thing: *state*, which it polls a few seconds behind. Sending a command over ADB is not slow — `am start` and `input keyevent` execute essentially instantly. So the split isn't fast-transport vs slow-transport; it's that each transport has a blind half. We use only the good half of each: state and navigation ride the push transport (`androidtv_remote`), launches and system keys ride ADB, and the laggy ADB state reading is never used at all. Nothing in the controller reads from `$context.system` — it only fires at it.

On the name: "system" was deliberate, and I'd defend it. The rule is that **roles name the job, transports are an implementation detail of the dialect**. The role vocabulary — media_player, dpad, power, volume, system — is the platform-neutral grammar every activity speaks. On Google TV the system channel *happens* to be ADB. On Tizen it might be a WebSocket API; on some future platform, a REST call. If we named the role "adb", every non-Android platform would either carry a lying role name or fork the vocabulary. "System" says what the channel is *for* — OS-level operations the media stack can't do: launching, settings, raw keycodes — and stays true on every platform.

Which brings you to the real question: **where is the command→device mapping actually specified?** It's a two-layer indirection, and each layer knows only one thing:

The **activity** knows *who* — role → entity. `system: media_player.deck_hisense_projector_adb_…`. It knows nothing about services or keycodes.

The **dialect** knows *how* — command → service + role. Every action in the googletv layer says `service: androidtv.adb_command, entity: $context.system, data: {command: …}`. It knows nothing about your house; `$context.system` is a hole the activity fills.

The engine just joins them at press-time: resolve `$context.system` through the current activity, call the service. So "Settings goes over ADB to the projector" is never written anywhere as one fact — the dialect says "Settings goes over `adb_command` to whoever holds the system role," and your activity says "the system role is held by the projector's ADB entity." That factoring is exactly what made purification possible: pull the second half out of the controller and the first half stays shippable.

The `routing:` block at the top of `dialects/googletv.yaml` is the human-readable summary of those choices — state→media_player, navigation→dpad, launch→system, system_keys→system — today documentation, machine-read in the bundles round so Studio can validate your wiring against it.

But why don't I have a system on all my other activities?

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T18:23:06.975Z
========================================================================

Because none of their dialects ask for one. A role only means something when the platform layer on the other end references it — and until v0.44, nothing anywhere said `$context.system`.

Walk the ladder on your existing devices. The Fire TV's launcher grammar (`firetv` class) is `source:` → `select_source` on `$context.media_player` — its ADB integration's media_player handles both state *and* launching, so one role covers both jobs. Same story for the Samsung (`tizen` class). One integration, one entity family, no split. The Google TV is the first platform where the jobs wouldn't fit down one pipe — good state and reliable commands live in *different integrations* — so it's the first dialect that needed a second channel, and that's the moment the role got invented.

And this is the roles system working as designed rather than an inconsistency: the role vocabulary is a *menu*, not a *form*. An activity wires the roles its destination controller consumes and skips the rest — hide-unwired means an unwired role costs nothing and an irrelevant one would just sit there dead. Adding `system` to Watch FireTV today would change nothing, because no tile in the firetv controller binds it.

The one forward-looking wrinkle: your Fire TV *does* have ADB (it shares the adbkey with the projector), so if we ever give the firetv controller a Device-keys section like the Google TV one, `system` becomes meaningful there too — and wiring it in your Watch FireTV activity at that point is a one-chip edit in Studio, no migration. That's also the shape of the phase-2 promise: once devices are first-class bundles, the *bundle* declares which roles it can fill, and Studio can tell you "this controller wants `system`; this device can provide it" instead of you carrying the map in your head.

**How would a user know it needs `system`?** Right now, they wouldn't. Hide-unwired is doing its job silently: wire nothing, and the Device-keys section simply doesn't exist. That's correct *enforcement* but zero *guidance* — you'd only discover the role by reading the controller yaml, which is exactly the kind of thing you learned by building it and a user never would. The missing piece is that a controller has an implicit contract — "I consume media_player, dpad, power, volume, system" — and nothing renders it.

The good news: that contract is already machine-derivable *today*, no new machinery. The controller yaml literally contains every `$context.*` reference. Studio could scan the view an activity's Navigate-to points at and show a **Consumes strip** on the activity card: each role the controller references, green when wired, hollow when not, with a one-liner like "system unwired → Device keys will hide." Not an error — unwired is legitimate — but the contract becomes visible at the moment you're wiring, instead of being discovered by absence on the remote.

**Where does it say what the roles map to?** Two places, both wrong for users: the `routing:` block in `dialects/googletv.yaml` (documentation, human-read only) and the action entries themselves (`$context.system` scattered through the view). The dialect is meant to graduate into the machine-read source of truth in the bundles round — routing, key catalogs, forbidden lists all feeding Studio. The Consumes strip is the first, cheapest slice of that.

**Are we mixing up the two layers?** The architecture keeps them separate; the *UI* currently doesn't show you the boundary. Cleanly:

- The **activity** is the device group: who's in the cast, which entity holds which role, plus experience policy (which controller to show, power behavior). It never says what buttons exist or what they fire.
- The **controller + dialect** are the remote UI mapping: what tiles appear, what each press sends, over which role. They never name an entity.

The join is one line — the activity's Navigate-to — and everything crosses it through role names. Nothing leaks in either direction (purification just proved that mechanically: `pureNoDefaults` asserts the controller side carries no entities). What's mixed up is only the *presentation*: the activity card is where you wire roles, but it gives you no view of what the chosen controller will do with them. Render the contract at the seam and the two layers stop feeling entangled.

Happy to build the Consumes strip — it's a Studio-only change, small, and it's the piece that would have answered today's `system` question for you without asking me. Want it in the next batch, or park it for the bundles round where it can read the dialect properly?

This is the right direction to walk, and your four steps are a cleaner spec than anything we've written down. Let me hold them up against what exists and where the gaps are.

**Steps 1–2: the user thinks in devices and a signal chain. Our cast is a flat entity list.** That's the first gap. Nobody thinks "I need `media_player.sts_samsung_q90_porch`" — they think "the Samsung," and the entity is a detail the system should fetch. And to your last question: yes, *within one integration* that pairing is already handled — HA's device registry knows `media_player.fire_tv_family…` and `remote.fire_tv_family…` are the same box (same device entry, same config entry; I verified the same structure on the projector yesterday). So the UI you deserve is: pick **Fire TV** once, and its media_player and remote come along automatically, sibling-lookup via the registry. What no integration can ever know is the *chain* — that the Fire TV feeds the Samsung feeds the soundbar. That's HDMI wiring in your living room; it exists only in your head. HA has no signal-chain concept at all. **The activity is precisely where that knowledge gets recorded** — that's its whole reason to exist. (One caveat the projector taught us: sometimes one physical device is *two* HA devices — androidtv_remote + ADB, unlinked, different MACs. So our device concept has to be allowed to span HA devices. That's exactly the phase-2 bundle.)

**Step 3 is the roles table read aloud.** "Media stuff on the Fire TV, source_select on the TV, volume on the soundbar, keys on the remote" — that sentence *is* `media_player → fire_tv, source_select → samsung, volume → soundbar, dpad/system → remote.fire_tv`. So the abstraction underneath is right; what's wrong is that we present it in engineering vocabulary. A user shouldn't meet the word "role." The UI should ask the questions your sentence answers: **Who plays it? Who switches inputs? Who makes the sound? Who takes the keys?** Same data model, human grammar.

**Step 4 — yes, and it half-exists.** The roles table on the activity card is that "separate UI area," but it's presented as an afterthought below the cast rather than as the main event. Working backwards from your steps, the flow should probably be a chain-builder: add devices in signal order (source → display → audio), and because each device's *position in the chain plus its domain* implies its jobs, we can prefill the whole mapping — source device gets playback/keys/apps, display gets input-switching, audio endpoint gets volume, and the user only touches the exceptions. Your step 3 then becomes something the user *confirms* rather than constructs. The Consumes strip from earlier is the validator on top: whatever controller this activity opens, show which questions it needs answered and which are still blank.

So the layering, UX-first: **the chain is the mental model → the bundle is how a device joins with its entities attached → the questions are how jobs get assigned → roles are just the storage format**, and users should never see the bottom layer.

None of this invalidates what's built — it says phase 2 isn't only "bundles as config plumbing," it's the moment the activity card gets re-founded on devices and plain-language job assignment. Want me to sketch that card as a mock (chain strip, the four questions, prefill heuristics) before we commit any engineering to it?

CLAUDE  2026-07-29T19:00:59.782Z
========================================================================

That's the Harmony wizard, and it's worth being explicit about why it worked: every question is one a user can answer *without knowing anything about protocols, entities, or transports* — they're all questions about the living room. And the magic underneath was that six living-room answers fully determined the engineering. Map them onto our primitives and the decomposition is almost eerily clean:

**Q1 (activity type)** → the controller + dialect. "Watch a Movie" implies the media-player anatomy, transport, dpad, an apps drawer; "Listen to Music" implies the music controller; "Custom" opens the raw editor. It also determines *which of the later questions even get asked* — a Listen activity never asks about a display. The type is a question-template.

**Q2 (devices involved)** → the cast — and it's device bundles by construction, never entities. This is why phase 2 has to come before any wizard: the wizard's vocabulary *is* devices.

**Q3–4 (which is the display / who does volume)** → role assignment, disguised as furniture questions. "Which device is the display" fills source_select and display-power; "who does volume" fills volume. The Fire TV never gets asked about because Q1+Q2 already imply it: the source device in a Watch activity takes playback, keys, and apps by default. Users only answer where ambiguity exists — exactly your prefill-and-confirm instinct from last message.

**Q5–6 (inputs)** → and here's the piece Harmonium doesn't own yet: **activity start-state**. That's not a role (roles are *who does a job during* the activity); it's *what state the world must be in when the activity begins* — Samsung to HDMI2, soundbar to D.IN. Today that knowledge lives in your HA-side scripts behind the activity select, hand-written. The wizard would let us *generate* it: power on every cast device, set each declared input, in order.

And once start-state is declared rather than scripted, we inherit Harmony's crown jewel almost for free: **the activity diff**. Harmony never blindly powered things off between activities — it compared the outgoing and incoming casts, powered off only devices leaving the stage, and re-inputted only devices whose input changed. We can do the same, because on a switch we hold both activities' declared states. The soundbar survives Watch→Listen untouched; the Fire TV goes to sleep. That's the behavior that made Harmony feel like magic to non-technical family members, and it falls out of the data model.

So the full stack, UX-first: **wizard answers → cast + roles + start-state → controller renders from roles, sequences generate from start-state, diffing from cast comparison.** Edge cases (shared devices, no-input devices, the projector's two-headed ADB situation, "none/ignore") slot in as wizard branches, not architecture changes.

This feels like it deserves to be captured while it's hot — a design doc laying out the wizard question flow, the answer→primitive mapping, the start-state schema, and the diff rules, so phase 2 (bundles) gets built knowing it's the wizard's foundation. Want me to write that up as `docs/wizard.md` and mirror it, before we touch any code?

| Now Playing | `media_player` | the media tile, transport, play/pause state |
| Navigation | `dpad` | arrows · select · back · home — physical remote keys pass through here |
| Power button | `power` | what the power key toggles |

Control name leads, mono role key sits beside it (it's the vocabulary you'll see in yaml anyway), effect line underneath. Precise and readable, no theater.

**On plural — here's where I'll push back, because I think the singular is load-bearing.** Your instinct that "who switches inputs" has multiple answers is correct *about the activity* but not *about the remote*. Two different things hide under that phrase:

*What the activity does to the world* — "set the Samsung to Fire TV AND the soundbar to D.IN when this starts." Genuinely plural, and it's **already plural in the UI**: the Inputs tab gives every sourced cast device its own row, and each answer becomes a step in the generated Start Action. Same for power: "turn several things off at the end" is the Actions checklist, per device.

*Where a control on the remote routes* — the Source tile shows **one** device's input list; a volume press lands on **one** entity; the power key toggles **one** thing. A button press has exactly one destination. That's why roles are singular, and it's not a limitation I'd engineer away — a Source tile mixing two devices' inputs into one list would be a genuinely worse remote.

So the real bug isn't that Jobs can't take plural answers — it's that my wording made Jobs *sound like* the activity-orchestration question, so it reads as a duplicate of Inputs with an arbitrary single-answer restriction. The two tabs need to declare their division of labor. One more idea riffing on your Consumes strip reaction: since we scan the controller's contract anyway, the Wiring tab could **lead with the rows the controller actually consumes** and fold the rest under "not used by this controller." The form becomes the contract. Counter-argument: wiring a role the current controller ignores is still meaningful if you switch controllers later, so it's a fold, never hidden.

**"The remote" was the wrong anchor.** You're right: remotes vary (Astrion has physical keys, a phone has none, a future wall panel has three buttons), and controllers vary too. The stable truth isn't "where buttons route" — it's older than that. Look at the vocabulary the tab already uses: **cast**, **primary**, **roles**. It's theater, and it's been theater since you named the cast. The activity is the *production*, the devices are the *actors*, and a role is a *part in this production*. The Samsung is capable of playing Volume Keys (it claims it), but in *Watch Fire TV* that part could go to the soundbar. The header should say exactly that:

> **Roles — which cast member plays each part in this activity** · *one device per role*

No remote, no buttons. The row labels (Now Playing, Navigation, Source picker) survive untouched because a part is *named by what it powers* — that's just what a part is. And the Consumes strip is the bridge to surfaces: "this controller consumes these parts." The chain reads cleanly: devices claim what they *can* do → the activity casts them and assigns who *does* do it → the controller consumes the parts it needs. Three layers, each sentence true regardless of which remote is in your hand.

**On "devices" — here I'll defend the word, because your HA instinct is exactly right and it lands in our favor.** In HA, a device is a physical thing exposing one or more entities. That is precisely what our library entry is — with one correction HA can't make: when a physical device shows up as *two* HA devices (the projector: androidtv_remote + ADB, unlinked, different MACs), our bundle glues them back into the one physical object they actually are. So our "device" isn't a new concept wearing a familiar word; it's **HA's device, repaired** — plus two kinds of annotation: *claims* (facts about the device: "my ADB media_player is the commands channel") and *traits* (facts about waking it: WOL, settle delay, never-off). Everything in the bundle is device-truth — true in every room, every activity.

Which is why I'd argue it's **not** an Activity Set. The test: does the information change per activity? A bundle's contents don't — the Samsung's WOL recipe and KEY_* codes are the same whether it's in Watch Fire TV or Watch Smart TV. What *does* change per activity is the casting and the role assignments — and that already has a home (the activity) and a name (the cast). And here's the kicker: the reusable-across-activities bundle you're intuiting — "this cast + this wiring, saved for reuse" — **also already exists**: it's the Setup snippet (Save as snippet on the Devices tab captures cast + wiring; Use snippet replays it into another activity). So the taxonomy is complete without a new noun: **device** = facts (library), **cast + roles** = choices (activity), **snippet** = saved choices (reusable). If we introduced "Activity Set" as a first-class thing, it would compete with two of those three.

Where I want your ruling: the header. My candidate is *"Roles — which cast member plays each part in this activity."* Alternatives if the theater flavor is too much: *"Roles — which device fills each role in this activity"* (plainer, slightly redundant) or *"Roles — who does what in this activity"* (shortest, but vaguer than the table below deserves). Activities don't create devices; they *cast* existing ones. Watch Fire TV casts three of them; Watch Smart TV casts two of the same three; nothing was minted either time. I think the "composite device for every activity?" feeling comes from two genuinely different composites hiding under one word, and it's worth splitting them permanently:

**Integration-composite** — *one physical object that HA fractured.* The projector is one thing on your deck; HA sees two devices (androidtv_remote + ADB) because a device in HA belongs to exactly one integration. Our library entry glues the fragments back into the physical object. This is what our "device" is — and there's exactly one per physical thing, ever.

**System-composite** — *several physical objects working as one experience.* "The porch TV setup": Fire TV + Samsung + soundbar. This is what you were reaching for back in the v0.44 discussion when you said Porch TV could be "a composite device." But notice it already has a name and a home: it's **the cast, and the activity is its container**. The activity page *is* the system-composite's control surface — which is exactly what you observed back then ("the Porch TV activity page is exactly what the Porch TV device page should be"). We don't need a second noun for it; we'd just be renaming the activity.

So the full grammar, one line: **HA gives us fragments → a device is the physical object reassembled → a cast is devices grouped for an experience → roles say who does what within it.** Each word used for exactly one thing.

On whether "device" itself needs replacing to keep distance from HA's word: my honest recommendation is no. Our device maps one-to-one onto what a normal human means by device — *the thing on the shelf* — and it's HA's usage that's the deviation (one per integration, not one per object). For your audience, a line of copy in the library kills the ambiguity better than a new noun would: **"one entry per physical device — even when HA splits it across several integrations."** That sentence is already almost there in the editor; I'd sharpen it to say "even when HA shows it as two or three devices." I think both trade a small ambiguity for a permanent whiff of jargon — HA users will translate "device" correctly after one reading, whereas "gear" needs translating forever. Your call: keep **Device** with the sharpened copy line, or rename?

This is the right thread to pull, and pulling it hard actually collapses the guesswork entirely. Let me take your three framings in turn.

**commands_A / commands_B — no, and here's the principled reason:** letters are roles with the semantics removed. The author who "has no clue" now has to wire *two* opaque slots instead of one. Whenever it feels like a role needs an A and a B, what's really happened is two different *meanings* are hiding under one name — and the fix is naming the meanings, not lettering the copies. But when I look for the second meaning here, it doesn't exist: on every platform we've touched, one device has one command channel (Google TV: ADB; Fire TV: ADB; Tizen: the media_player's own websocket). Nothing needs `commands_B`. If some future device genuinely grows a second channel — an IR blaster side-door, say — the dialect names it semantically that day.

**"The author of the activity will have no clue" — correct, and that sentence should be a design law, not a complaint.** The author's required clue-count must be zero. Watch who actually holds each piece of knowledge: the *dialect* knows that Google TV launches must ride `androidtv.adb_command` and that this service only accepts an `androidtv`-integration media_player. The *device* knows which of its member entities that is. The *activity* should know nothing — cast the projector, roles prefill, done. That's your "this should be handled by our googletv config," and it's exactly the machine-read-dialect promise coming due. Concretely: the dialect file grows a declaration —

```yaml
channels:
  commands: { integration: androidtv, domain: media_player }
```

— and here's the part that kills the guesswork you smelled: **right now the seeder guesses the ADB twin by name-regex** (`_adb_` in the entity id). That's the "too much guesswork" — you're right, it's brittle and it's fake knowledge. The true discriminator is a *fact HA already holds*: the entity's integration platform. Your projector's two media_players are `androidtv_remote` vs `androidtv` in the entity registry — I verified exactly this on your HA two days ago. The Studio just can't see it yet, because it only reads `/api/states`, which doesn't carry platform. The fix is small plumbing: Studio fetches the entity registry once at load (one websocket call with the token it already holds), and then the chain is fact all the way down — dialect declares "commands = the `androidtv` media_player," seeder resolves it by registry lookup instead of name-sniffing, and a device claiming `app_class: googletv` whose commands claim *isn't* an androidtv entity gets a visible warning chip: "this entity can't take adb_command."

**Explicit "adb" — yes in the UI, no in the vocabulary.** The role stays `commands` because Tizen's command channel isn't ADB and the role vocabulary is platform-neutral. But once the dialect declares the channel, the Roles row can stop being coy: the commands candidate renders as "Pergola Projector · **ADB channel** ✓" — the platform-specific truth as annotation, verified against the registry, exactly where the author's eyes are. Best of both: neutral grammar, concrete label.

So v0.45.2 becomes a coherent package: the unified cast picker (your flow — library, implied `⊞` bundles, loose entities, silent minting), the snippet buttons renamed to "Save cast as set… / Use a set…", the dialect `channels:` declaration, registry-backed seeding replacing the `_adb_` regex, and the mismatch warning. The activity author's experience at the end of it: type "projector," pick `⊞ Pergola Projector`, watch every role fill itself — including commands, correctly, for reasons they never need to learn. Green light?

The end-state your question implies is the one we parked as phase 3, and I think it's ready to come off the shelf:

**One TV Player controller.** Stock, pure $context, platform-agnostic. Its Device-keys section becomes a *generator tile* — `{type: keys}` — exactly parallel to the apps drawer: at render time the engine reads the active dialect's key catalog and expands one preset tile per verified key, each firing through the `commands` channel the dialect declares. Fire TV activity → Fire TV's keys appear. Projector activity → Settings/Search/All apps/Quick settings/Live TV. Tizen → whatever tizen declares, or nothing, and the section hides itself (hide-unwired's cousin: hide-when-dialect-silent). The key catalogs move from the design-record file into the machine-read dialect entries where `channels:` already lives. **Adding platform #4 becomes a pure data exercise** — channels + keys + apps in one yaml block, zero new views — which is the shippable-product test your purification ruling set up.

Google TV Player then dissolves. Its controller entry retires, activities point at TV Player, and the forbidden-keys list finally gets its intended job: gating what the catalog may offer, as guardrail data rather than comments.

**On the name — you're right, and I'd go further than "Player dialect."** `app_class` was named in v0.30 when it only launched apps. Dialect — and I can make the case against the other two concretely.

**`class`** is already taken twice inside Harmonium itself: screens carry `class: room` / `class: activity`, and the apps generator tile carries `class: googletv` today. Overloading it a third time means "class" in the yaml would mean three different things depending on where you're standing. It's also the most collision-prone word in software generally. Disqualified on internal grounds alone.

**`device class`** reads instantly — but it collides head-on with HA, and with exactly the audience you've told me to design for. `device_class` in HA is a specific, ubiquitous attribute (`tv`, `speaker`, `temperature`...) that appears in every entity's attributes — we even fetch and store it in the Studio's entity picker data right now. An HA-comfortable user seeing "Device class: Google TV" will reasonably assume it's HA's `device_class`, wonder why the values look wrong, and go check. That's the same trap as bare "devices" was, except this time the colliding meaning is *pervasive* in HA rather than occasional. (Awkward confession: the Apps editor's own copy currently says "device class" — that predates this week and would get aligned regardless of the pick.)

**`dialect`** costs one sentence of learning and then never collides with anything — not in HA, not in Harmonium, not in general software vocabulary. And it's semantically the most honest of the three: the thing isn't a *classification* of the device, it's the *vocabulary you speak to it* — which keys exist, how launches ride, which channel carries commands, what's forbidden. Two devices of the same "class" in any normal sense (two TVs) speak different dialects; that's the entire point of the concept. It's also already the load-bearing word across the docs, the dialects/ folder, and every design conversation we've had — the rename would make the code match how we actually talk about it.

So: `dialect` as the config key, "Dialect" in the UI, effect line "the platform's vocabulary — keys, launches, channels." Say the word and it goes into the v0.46 scope with the healer alongside the TV Player collapse.

v0.47.7 shipped and mirrored (studio-only: bat + hard refresh when convenient). The "⚙ From primary device" button now sits beside "⚙ From inputs" on the State tab — for Watch Projector, one click and the tile follows the projector's actual power.

**#3 deserves a full answer, because the design is subtler than it looks.** The select is **not** a claim that only one thing is happening — it's a *spotlight*: it names what this room's remote is currently driving. Keys, volume, context, the controller's fill — all follow the spotlight. One spotlight per room, because a remote can only point at one experience at a time; separate rooms have separate selects and run concurrently without interacting.

Now your scenario — music playing with the TV on in the background, same room: **device-rule states are independent of the select.** Music's state derives from the Sonos (`any_state: playing/paused…`), Watch Fire TV's derives from the Samsung + its input. Both rules true → *both tiles show ON simultaneously* on the room page, truthfully. The select merely decides which of them owns the buttons right now. Tap the other tile to move the spotlight — `confirm_switch` asks first, the incoming Start runs (safe over any prior state, per the never-guess-power doctrine — so switching to music doesn't touch the TV), and nothing stops the outgoing activity unless a Stop action says so. That's Harmony's model minus Harmony's sin: multiple things can *be* on; one thing at a time is *in hand*.

The one discipline this asks of you: multi-ON display only works for activities whose state comes from *devices*. A select-based activity can't show ON while the spotlight is elsewhere — the select is single-valued. Which is exactly why the two generators exist: "From inputs" for display-routed activities, "From primary device" for things that genuinely power off. Give music and Watch Projector device-derived state and your background-music scenario renders correctly today.

v0.48 shipped — and your #6 and #7 turned out to be **one bug**. The HA log had it: the generated Start's `harmonium.set_activity` step carried no `workspace`, so it defaulted to `main` — which has no `new_room_watch_projector`. The script died at step 1: no wake, no select flip, and a 500 for both ▶ Test and the tap. Two-layer fix: `harmonium.run` now stamps its own workspace onto any nested harmonium step (recursing into if/then blocks, never touching the stored config), and `set_activity` with no workspace now *finds the owner* across all workspaces — so your own automations never need to know workspaces exist.

And your ruling is law regardless: **the tap is the intent**. `startActivity` now marks the tapped activity pending, and the player renders as that activity from that moment — even if the start action fails outright, you get the full controller showing the projector's true off state. The "No activity is active" page can only ever greet someone wandering in from the sidebar. New `pendingFill` test proves it: start fails → player filled, no hint, and a confirming select still outranks pending.

The Studio round: confirmed — pre-wired is a convenience, never a requirement, and "loose" is gone (the picker now says "cast this entity"). The tab bar grew a **Preview: Controller · Room page** toggle so you can flip to the page view without closing the card (controller stays the default each open). The picker moved below the directly-cast entity rows, tabs are now 13.5px semibold with a thick accent bar (first-class citizens), and the circled misalignment was the Navigate-to select wearing different styling than every other field (plus a one-sided hint shoving its neighbor up with `items-end`) — both normalized.

All 14 suites green; G:\ and S:\ hash-verified, Projects pushed. **Ceremony: this round touches `__init__.py`** — so it's bat run, HA restart, then the 🚀 deploy script and a Studio hard refresh.
