v0.48.1 shipped — all six, mirrored and verified (G:\ + S:\ hash-matched, Projects pushed). The answers, in your order:

**1 + 2 — Power now means the activity.** The on-screen bar's ⏻ was doing raw `homeassistant.toggle` on `$context.power` — that's what stranded your select. Now it toggles the *activity*: running → end with the standard two-press confirm; not running → the full generated start sequence. Select and devices move together. Physical short-press power keeps the control-target policy (device power stays a deliberate physical gesture). And for browser navigation: ⌂ **Home** and a red ⏻ **End** now live in the title bar — always reachable, never crowding the grid, and hidden on physical-key remotes. The ← was already there; now it has company.

**6 — The flakiness had a name: implied state.** Your Watch Projector had no state rule, so truth was the select — which goes stale the moment anything touches a device behind its back. Now an activity with *no authored rule* derives truth live from its primary device's player. Projector off → tile says Off, whatever the select claims — and tapping it then *starts* rather than opens. Fire TV activities are exempt by their own `never_off` trait (its state can't witness anything), and an authored rule always wins. The State tab now says "Implied — primary device's player (default)" so this isn't invisible magic.

**3** — Active tab: size bump + `--color-tile` lift, exactly as specced; the directly-cast rows dropped to `--color-bg` with a 1px `--color-line` border. **4** — The toggle wasn't dead, it was mute: it controls whether the cast lists itself as the Devices section on the controller, but it never pushed the preview, so you saw nothing. Your three symptoms, three causes:

The cache key is now `(type:id)` and the request always sends the id — empty included — whenever a node is named. **The junk drawer** — Camera, TTS, images, Radio Browser are HA's `media-source://` entries merged into every player's root; they're the *server's* media, not the player's library. They're now hidden at the root **by default**, identified by id prefix (a fact, not a title list), which on your Sonos leaves exactly Favorites + Music Library — with zero configuration. And per your ruling it's data, not code: `media_sources: true` on the browse tile brings them back, and `include: [Favorites, Music Library]` narrows further if you ever want to — advisory, so it can never blank another player whose tree uses different words.

**The "N"** — that's the SONOS wordmark being center-cropped by `object-fit: cover` to its middle letter. Browse thumbnails now render contained on a small light chip.

CLAUDE  2026-07-31T22:59:46.336Z
========================================================================

Keymaps live in two places that are really one:

**Source of truth: `yaml/system.yaml`** — it has a `keymaps:` block (named maps of *raw key event → logical button*, e.g. `"[": back`, `F2: power`) and a `remotes:` block of hardware profiles. Each profile bundles three things: `capabilities` (what the hardware physically has — `physical_dpad`, `physical_volume`, `touch`, `pointer`), a `keymap` reference, and optionally `fully: true` to mark the kiosk. Yours today: `default` (browser: touch+pointer) and `astrion` (physical dpad+volume, whose keymap re-points `]`/`;`/`=` at the hold variants because Fully injects those for long-presses). The compiler resolves this into `config.remotes`, and in the Studio it's **System → Remotes & keymaps** (each non-main workspace carries its own copy).

**How a given screen knows which profile it is:** at boot the engine resolves, in order — a one-time `#device=<name>` hash on the URL (stored in the browser, so you provision a device once), else Fully Kiosk auto-detection (`window.fully` → the first profile with `fully: true`), else `default`. So the *same workspace URL* — `main/index.html` — shows Listen to Music in your browser as `default` and on the Astrion as `astrion`. Workspace and remote profile are orthogonal: the URL picks the world, the profile picks the hardware personality.

**"Different keys available" is then handled at two layers:**

*Capabilities gate the UI.* Tiles and chrome declare `only:`/`unless:` conditions — the on-screen d-pad shows `unless: physical_dpad`, the title-bar ⌂/⏻ appear only on touch-only clients, the hardware-button bar shows `only: physical_dpad`. That's why the browser gets soft controls the Astrion doesn't need.

*The keymap translates whatever arrives.* Everything downstream — input policy, control_target, hold roles, dialects — speaks only logical buttons (`up`, `select`, `back`, `power_hold`, `ch_up`…). A remote's profile just maps its raw emissions onto that vocabulary.

**So for a Haptique RS90** it depends on how it reaches the frontend. If it pairs as a Bluetooth keyboard/HID to the device running Harmonium, it's exactly one new block in system.yaml: add a `haptique` keymap with whatever key codes its buttons emit, a `haptique` profile with its honest capabilities, and open the remote once with `#device=haptique`. Missing buttons cost nothing — unmapped logical buttons just never fire, and the capability flags make the UI compensate (no `physical_volume` → volume tiles stay prominent). But if the RS90 talks to *Home Assistant* directly through its own hub/integration rather than to the screen, its buttons never hit our keymap at all — they'd land as HA events/automations, which you'd point at the same targets (`harmonium.run`, activity toggles, `media_player` services). Worth checking which mode it actually supports before wiring; the first path is zero new code, the second is authored in HA, not Harmonium.

One honest gap if you go multi-remote seriously: the Studio's keymap editor edits the maps, but there's no "press a key and I'll tell you its code" capture helper — adding an unknown remote means finding its codes (the ⓘ boot flash shows recent key events, which helps). If the RS90 lands on your desk, that capture wizard would be the natural next build.

========================================================================

Good example to stress-test the grammar with — and it exposes exactly one real gap. Here's the honest picture.

**What the setup would look like** — three layers, matching how back/home/power holds already work:

*Layer 1 — the Astrion shell.* The field lesson baked into input.js: injected keys don't deliver reliable keyup timing to the webview, so **holds are the shell's job** — KeyMapper long-press mappings send *distinct* keys. So on the Astrion you'd map dpad-left long-press to inject an unused key (say `,`) and dpad-right long-press to `.` — same move as your existing `]`/`;`/`=` hold mappings.

*Layer 2 — the keymap.* In system.yaml (or Studio → Remotes & keymaps), the astrion map grows `",": left_hold` and `".": right_hold`. Pure data.

*Layer 3 — the bindings.* Each player view binds the logical button, exactly like music already binds `ch_up` to next-track:

```yaml
# music.yaml
buttons:
  left_hold:  { seek: -15, entity: $context.media_player }
  right_hold: { seek: 15, entity: $context.media_player }
# tv.yaml — the Fire TV speaks remote commands, not seek
buttons:
  right_hold: { service: remote.send_command, entity: $context.dpad,
                data: { command: FAST_FORWARD } }
```

**The gap: layer 3 doesn't fully exist yet.** Two small engine pieces are missing. First, the button vocabulary is *closed* — the `act()` switch routes the known names, and the screen-`buttons` lookup only runs for vol/ch/mute/menu_hold; an arriving `left_hold` would fall through the switch and vanish. The fix is small and doctrine-clean: any logical button with a binding in the screen/global `buttons` map runs its action — open vocabulary, bindings win, unknown-and-unbound stays a no-op. Second, **relative seek doesn't exist as an action** — HA's `media_player.media_seek` is absolute-position only, and there's no universal rewind service for music players. But the engine already tracks live `media_position` (it interpolates it for the progress bar), so a `{seek: ±N}` action that computes position and calls `media_seek` is cheap and works on Sonos and MA alike. Both pieces together are a small round; say go and I'll build them, wire the music/TV views, and add the two astrion keymap entries — the KeyMapper long-press mappings on the tablet itself are the one part that's yours.

**On the capture helper** — not baking anything, but here's my thinking. Your two ideas (a capture tile that fills the page and scrolls; an option on a blank page) can both fall out of one move for free: make capture a **virtual screen**, like the queue is. `queue:` taught us the pattern — no config authoring needed, it's just an address. A `keys:` screen would be a one-column scrolling list, newest press on top, each row showing the raw key/code plus what the current keymap resolves it to — with *unmapped* rows highlighted, since those are the ones you're hunting when learning a new remote. Then your "tile on a page" is just a nav tile pointing at it (delete it when the RS90 is wired), and it can also live permanently behind the ⓘ menu in the title bar — a diagnostic surface the family never trips over, which is where I'd put the default entry. The groundwork exists: the `#debug=1` card already captures raw events in the capture phase before the engine touches them; this is that card grown up into a screen. The one thing capture can't be is Studio-side — the keys have to be pressed *on the device the remote is paired to* — so "read the codes off the screen, type them into the keymap editor" stays the honest flow, and a fancier auto-learn round-trip through the integration is a later cleverness if hand-typing ever gets old.

It's in the Studio's right-hand column — the one with the phone preview. Step by step:

1. Hard-refresh the Studio first (Ctrl+Shift+R) — without that you're still on the old build.
2. Open any **page editor** (e.g. click Porch in the left nav). This matters: on the workspace **Map** view the preview column is hidden entirely, so there's no soft remote there at all.
3. Look at the right column, under the phone: the keypad, then the ✚ HOLD bar, and **below that a small grey caption**: "Soft remote sends the 'default' profile's real keys. **✎ edit layout**" — the orange link is what you click. On a shorter window you may need to scroll that right column down to see it.

Once you click it: every key slot turns into a dropdown — set the bottom row to 🔇 MUTE / — / ≡ MENU for your example (— is the blank). ✕ at a row's right edge removes the row, "＋ row" adds one, "reset" restores the stock arrangement. Hit **Done** to go back to live buttons, then **Save & Deploy** — the layout is stored on the remote profile in the workspace config, so it persists like any other edit.

One subtlety: the layout belongs to the profile selected in the "Preview as" dropdown at the top of that column. Edit while previewing as `default` and you're shaping the browser remote; switch to `astrion` first if you want to shape that one.
